The distance from a point to a coordinate **axis** is measured perpendicular to that axis,
so the coordinate **along** the axis plays no part.
**Step 1 — drop the perpendicular.** From P(a, b, c) the foot of the perpendicular on the
x-axis keeps the x-coordinate and sets the other two to zero:
**M = (a, 0, 0)**
**Step 2 — apply the distance formula.**
PM = √[(a − a)² + (b − 0)² + (c − 0)²]
= √(0 + b² + c²)
= **√(b² + c²)** ✓
**The rule in words.** The distance from a point to a coordinate **axis** uses the
**other two** coordinates:
distance from the **x-axis** = √(b² + c²)
distance from the **y-axis** = √(a² + c²)
distance from the **z-axis** = √(a² + b²)
**Contrast with a coordinate plane**, which uses only **one** coordinate:
distance to the **yz-plane** (x = 0) = |a|
distance to the **zx-plane** (y = 0) = |b|
distance to the **xy-plane** (z = 0) = |c|
and the distance to the **origin** uses all three: √(a² + b² + c²).
**A worked instance.** For P(3, 4, 12):
distance from the x-axis = √(16 + 144) = √160 ≈ **12·65**
distance from the y-axis = √(9 + 144) = √153 ≈ **12·37**
distance from the z-axis = √(9 + 16) = **5**
distance from the origin = √(9 + 16 + 144) = **13**
and each axis distance is less than the distance to the origin ✓ as it must be, since the
foot of the perpendicular is nearer than the origin.
**Reading the distractors.** **√(a² + c²)** is the distance from the **y**-axis and
**√(a² + b²)** from the **z**-axis — each the answer to a neighbouring question. And **a**
alone is the distance to the **yz-plane**. The letter that is *absent* from the answer
names the axis: a is missing here, and the axis is the **x**-axis ✓
∴ √(b² + c²).

The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so its slope is **−1/(dy/dx)** evaluated at
the point.
**Step 1 — write the function with a negative index**, which makes differentiating easier.
y = x² − 1/x² = **x² − x⁻²**
**Step 2 — differentiate.**
dy/dx = 2x − (−2)x⁻³
= **2x + 2/x³**
**Step 3 — evaluate at x = −1.**
dy/dx = 2(−1) + 2/(−1)³
= −2 + 2/(−1)
= −2 − 2
= **−4**
This is the slope of the **tangent**.
**Step 4 — take the negative reciprocal** for the normal:
slope of normal = −1/(−4) = **1/4** ✓
**Check that the point lies on the curve.** At x = −1:
y = (−1)² − 1/(−1)² = 1 − 1 = **0** ✓ so (−1, 0) really is on the curve, as the question
states.
**Why the sign works out positive.** The tangent slope is **negative** (−4), so the normal
slope, being its negative reciprocal, must be **positive** ✓ That observation alone rules
out options (2) and (4), both negative.
**Why the magnitude is 1/4 and not 4.** The normal's slope is the **reciprocal** of 4 in
size, not 4 itself. Option (3), 4, is what comes of taking the negative of the tangent
slope instead of the negative reciprocal — the commonest error in this topic.
**The two slopes in full.**
tangent at (−1, 0): slope **−4**, equation y − 0 = −4(x + 1), that is **4x + y + 4 = 0**
normal at (−1, 0): slope **1/4**, equation y = (1/4)(x + 1), that is **x − 4y + 1 = 0**
and the product of the slopes is (−4)(1/4) = **−1** ✓ confirming perpendicularity.
**A caution with the negative index.** d(x⁻²)/dx = −2x⁻³, so subtracting it gives
**+2x⁻³** — two minus signs making a plus. Getting that sign wrong gives
dy/dx = −2 + 2 = 0 and no normal slope at all.
∴ 1/4.

to it — found by dropping a perpendicular and solving.
**Step 1 — find the slope of the perpendicular.** The line x + y = 4 has slope **−1**, so
the perpendicular from (2, 4) has slope
m = −1/(−1) = **1**
**Step 2 — write the perpendicular line** through (2, 4):
y − 4 = 1(x − 2)
**y = x + 2**
**Step 3 — solve the two lines simultaneously.** Substituting into x + y = 4:
x + (x + 2) = 4
2x = 2
**x = 1**, and then **y = 1 + 2 = 3**
foot = **(1, 3)** ✓
**Check it is on the given line.** 1 + 3 = **4** ✓
**Check the perpendicularity.** The segment from (2, 4) to (1, 3) has slope
(3 − 4)/(1 − 2) = (−1)/(−1) = **1**, and (1)(−1) = **−1** ✓ perpendicular to x + y = 4.
**The formula route.** For the line ax + by + c = 0 and the point (x₀, y₀), the foot is
(x₀, y₀) − [(ax₀ + by₀ + c)/(a² + b²)](a, b)
Here a = 1, b = 1, c = −4 and (x₀, y₀) = (2, 4):
ax₀ + by₀ + c = 2 + 4 − 4 = **2**, and a² + b² = **2**
foot = (2, 4) − (2/2)(1, 1) = (2, 4) − (1, 1) = **(1, 3)** ✓ in one line.
**A quick filter on the options.** The foot must lie **on** x + y = 4, so its coordinates
must sum to 4:
**(3, −1):** 3 − 1 = 2 ✗
**(2, 2):** 2 + 2 = 4 ✓ passes this test
**(4, 0):** 4 + 0 = 4 ✓ passes too
**(1, 3):** 1 + 3 = 4 ✓

(2, 4) to (2, 2) the segment is vertical ✗ and to (4, 0) the slope is (0 − 4)/(4 − 2) =
**−2** ✗ Only (1, 3) gives slope 1.
**The distance, for interest.** |2 + 4 − 4|/√2 = 2/√2 = **√2**, and indeed the distance
from (2, 4) to (1, 3) is √(1 + 1) = √2 ✓
∴ (1, 3).

**normal**, so it is simply a multiple of the normal vector.
**Step 1 — read the normal.** The plane 2x − 3y + 4z = 29 has normal
**n̄ = (2, −3, 4)**
**Step 2 — write the foot as a multiple of it.** The foot F lies on the line through the
origin in the direction n̄:
**F = t(2, −3, 4) = (2t, −3t, 4t)**
**Step 3 — make F satisfy the plane.**
2(2t) − 3(−3t) + 4(4t) = 29
4t + 9t + 16t = 29

F = (2, −3, 4) ✓

is a multiple of the normal ✓ so OF is perpendicular to the plane.

**29** exactly, which makes t = 1 and the foot equal to the normal vector itself. The
question is built around that coincidence.
**The general formula.** For the plane ax + by + cz = d, the foot of the perpendicular
from the origin is
**(ad/(a²+b²+c²), bd/(a²+b²+c²), cd/(a²+b²+c²))**
= (2 × 29/29, −3 × 29/29, 4 × 29/29) = **(2, −3, 4)** ✓
and the perpendicular distance is |d|/√(a²+b²+c²) = 29/√29 = **√29** ✓ which matches

**(5, −1, 4)** ✗ not proportional
**(7, −1, 3)** ✗
**(5, −2, 3)** ✗

Reflecting a point in the **XY plane** leaves x and y alone and reverses the sign of
**z**.
**Why.** The XY plane is the set of points with **z = 0**. A reflection in it maps each
point to the point directly opposite through that plane: the perpendicular from (α, β, γ)
to the plane runs parallel to the z-axis, meets the plane at (α, β, 0), and continuing the
same distance beyond gives
**(α, β, −γ)** ✓
**Checking the two defining properties.**
**The midpoint lies in the mirror plane.** The midpoint of (α, β, γ) and (α, β, −γ) is
(α, β, (γ − γ)/2) = **(α, β, 0)**, whose z-coordinate is 0 ✓
**The segment is perpendicular to the plane.** The segment runs from (α, β, γ) to
(α, β, −γ), a direction of (0, 0, −2γ) — parallel to the **z-axis**, which is normal to
the XY plane ✓
**The full set of reflections**, worth laying out together:
in the **XY plane** (z = 0): (α, β, γ) → **(α, β, −γ)**
in the **YZ plane** (x = 0): → (−α, β, γ)
in the **ZX plane** (y = 0): → (α, −β, γ)
in the **x-axis**: → (α, −β, −γ)
in the **y-axis**: → (−α, β, −γ)
in the **z-axis**: → (−α, −β, γ)
in the **origin**: → (−α, −β, −γ)
The pattern: reflecting in a **plane** flips the **one** coordinate not named by the
plane; reflecting in an **axis** flips the **two** coordinates not named by it; and
reflecting in the origin flips all three.
**Reading the distractors.**
**(α, β, 0)** ✗ — this is the **foot** of the perpendicular, the projection onto the
plane, not the reflection. The reflection is **twice** as far.
**(0, 0, γ)** ✗ — the projection onto the **z-axis**.
**(−α, −β, γ)** ✗ — the reflection in the **z-axis**, which flips the other two.
The distinction between a projection and a reflection is what the first distractor is
testing, and it is the one most often chosen by mistake.
∴ (α, β, −γ).

The type of conic cut from a double cone depends on how the plane's angle **β** compares
with the cone's semi-vertical angle **α**.
**The classification.** With α the semi-vertical angle of the cone and β the angle the
cutting plane makes with the axis:
**β = 90°** → **circle** (the plane is perpendicular to the axis)
**α < β < 90°** → **ellipse**
**β = α** → **parabola** (the plane is parallel to a generator)
**0 ≤ β < α** → **hyperbola** (the plane is steep enough to meet **both** nappes)
**Statement I: "When α > β ≥ 0, the section is a hyperbola."** ✓ **TRUE**
This is exactly the last line of the table. When the plane is steeper than the cone's own
slope, it cuts through both the upper and lower nappes, and the two branches of a
hyperbola appear ✓
**Statement II: "When β > 90°, the section is an ellipse."** ✗ **FALSE**
β is the angle between the plane and the **axis**, and such an angle is measured in
[0°, 90°] — it cannot **exceed** 90°. At β = 90° exactly the plane is perpendicular to the
axis and the section is a **circle**, not an ellipse; and beyond 90° there is nothing to
describe. The ellipse arises for **α < β < 90°**, which is strictly **less** than 90° ✗
**Step — conclude.** Statement I is true and Statement II is false ✓
**The picture behind the table.** Imagine tilting a plane that starts horizontal:
horizontal (β = 90°) — the section is a **circle**
tilt a little — the circle stretches into an **ellipse**, and it remains closed as long
as the plane is less steep than the cone's side
tilt until the plane is exactly parallel to a generator (β = α) — the curve opens out into
a **parabola**, no longer closed
tilt further (β < α) — the plane now also catches the opposite nappe, and the section
becomes a two-branched **hyperbola**
**The degenerate cases.** If the plane passes through the **vertex**, the same four angles
give a point, a point, a single line and a pair of intersecting lines respectively — the
degenerate conics.
∴ Statement I is true, Statement II is false.

With A + B + C = 180°, the half-angles satisfy a standard identity.
**Step 1 — halve the angle sum.**
A + B + C = 180°
(A + B)/2 = 90° − C/2
**Step 2 — take the tangent of both sides.**
tan[(A + B)/2] = tan(90° − C/2) = **cot(C/2)**
**Step 3 — expand the left side** with the compound-angle formula, writing
t_A = tan(A/2) and so on:
(t_A + t_B)/(1 − t_A t_B) = 1/t_C
**Step 4 — cross-multiply.**
t_C(t_A + t_B) = 1 − t_A t_B
t_A t_C + t_B t_C = 1 − t_A t_B
**t_A t_B + t_B t_C + t_C t_A = 1** ✓
which is exactly the cyclic sum asked for:
**Σ tan(A/2) tan(B/2) = 1** ✓
**Check with an equilateral triangle.** A = B = C = 60°, so each half-angle is 30° and
tan 30° = 1/√3:
sum = 3 × (1/√3)(1/√3) = 3 × 1/3 = **1** ✓
**Check with a right triangle.** Take A = 90°, B = 60°, C = 30°, so the half-angles are
45°, 30°, 15°:
tan 45° = 1, tan 30° = 0·5774, tan 15° = 0·2679
sum = (1)(0·5774) + (0·5774)(0·2679) + (0·2679)(1)
= 0·5774 + 0·1547 + 0·2679
= **1·000** ✓
Two very different triangles, the same answer — which is what makes it an identity rather
than a coincidence.
**The companion identities**, all consequences of A + B + C = 180°:
**tan A + tan B + tan C = tan A tan B tan C**
**Σ tan(A/2)tan(B/2) = 1** ✓ (this question)
**Σ cot(A/2) = Π cot(A/2)**
**sin 2A + sin 2B + sin 2C = 4 sin A sin B sin C**
Each follows from the same substitution, replacing one angle by 180° minus the other two.
**Why 0 is offered.** It is the answer to Σ cos(A + B) type expressions, and to several
other cyclic sums — but here the identity gives exactly 1, independent of the triangle.
∴ 1.

The matrix is a **rotation matrix**, whose inverse is simply its **transpose** — but the
2 × 2 formula gives the same answer directly.
**Step 1 — compute the determinant.** With
M = [[cos 2θ, −sin 2θ], [sin 2θ, cos 2θ]]
|M| = (cos 2θ)(cos 2θ) − (−sin 2θ)(sin 2θ)
= cos²2θ + sin²2θ
= **1**
A determinant of 1 means the inverse is just the **adjugate**, with no division needed.
**Step 2 — write the adjugate.** For [[a, b], [c, d]] the adjugate is [[d, −b], [−c, a]]:
swap the diagonal entries, negate the off-diagonal ones. With a = cos 2θ, b = −sin 2θ,
c = sin 2θ, d = cos 2θ:
adj M = [[cos 2θ, **sin 2θ**], [**−sin 2θ**, cos 2θ]]
**Step 3 — divide by the determinant**, which is 1:
**M⁻¹ = [[cos 2θ, sin 2θ], [−sin 2θ, cos 2θ]]** ✓
**Check by multiplying.**
M M⁻¹ = [[cos 2θ, −sin 2θ], [sin 2θ, cos 2θ]] × [[cos 2θ, sin 2θ], [−sin 2θ, cos 2θ]]
top-left: cos²2θ + sin²2θ = **1**
top-right: cos 2θ sin 2θ − sin 2θ cos 2θ = **0**
bottom-left: sin 2θ cos 2θ − cos 2θ sin 2θ = **0**
bottom-right: sin²2θ + cos²2θ = **1**
= the identity matrix ✓
**The rotation reading.** M rotates the plane anticlockwise through the angle **2θ**. Its
inverse must rotate **back**, by −2θ, and
R(−2θ) = [[cos(−2θ), −sin(−2θ)], [sin(−2θ), cos(−2θ)]]
= **[[cos 2θ, sin 2θ], [−sin 2θ, cos 2θ]]** ✓ the same matrix, since cosine is even and
sine is odd. So the inverse is obtained by replacing θ with −θ, which simply moves the
minus sign from the top row to the bottom.
**Why M⁻¹ = Mᵀ here.** A rotation matrix is **orthogonal**: its columns are perpendicular
unit vectors, so MᵀM = I and the inverse is the transpose. Transposing swaps the
off-diagonal entries, which is exactly what happened ✓
**Reading the distractors.** Option (1) is **M itself**; option (3) has lost the minus
sign altogether, giving a matrix of determinant cos²2θ − sin²2θ = cos 4θ, not 1; and
option (2) has the sign on the wrong entry. Only one option moves the minus from the top
row to the bottom ✓
∴ [[cos 2θ, sin 2θ], [−sin 2θ, cos 2θ]].

The condition x + 1/x = 2 cos α identifies x as a point on the **unit circle** in the
complex plane, and then De Moivre's theorem does the rest.
**Step 1 — solve for x.** Multiplying by x,
x² − 2x cos α + 1 = 0
By the quadratic formula,
x = [2cos α ± √(4cos²α − 4)]/2
= cos α ± √(cos²α − 1)
= cos α ± √(−sin²α)
= **cos α ± i sin α**
so x = e^(±iα), a complex number of modulus **1**.
**Step 2 — raise to the n-th power** using De Moivre's theorem:
xⁿ = (cos α ± i sin α)ⁿ = **cos nα ± i sin nα**
**Step 3 — find 1/xⁿ.** Since |x| = 1, the reciprocal is the conjugate:
1/xⁿ = **cos nα ∓ i sin nα**
**Step 4 — add.** The imaginary parts cancel:
xⁿ + 1/xⁿ = (cos nα ± i sin nα) + (cos nα ∓ i sin nα)
= **2 cos nα** ✓
**Check with n = 1.** The formula gives 2 cos α ✓ which is the given condition — a
consistency check that the answer is right at least in the base case.
**Check with n = 2.** Squaring the given relation:
(x + 1/x)² = 4cos²α
x² + 2 + 1/x² = 4cos²α
x² + 1/x² = 4cos²α − 2 = 2(2cos²α − 1) = **2 cos 2α** ✓ by the double-angle formula,
matching the general result with n = 2.
**The recurrence hiding here.** Writing yₙ = xⁿ + 1/xⁿ, multiplying y₁ by yₙ gives
yₙ₊₁ = y₁yₙ − yₙ₋₁, that is **2cos(n+1)α = 2cos α · 2cos nα − 2cos(n−1)α** — the standard
Chebyshev recurrence, and another way to generate the result without complex numbers at
all.
**Reading the distractors.**
**2ⁿ cos α** and **2ⁿ cos nα** ✗ — the 2 is **not** raised to the power n. Only the angle
is multiplied by n; the factor 2 comes from adding two equal cosines and stays 2.
**2i sin nα** ✗ — this is x^n **minus** 1/xⁿ, where the real parts cancel instead. The
sign between the terms decides which part survives, and the question asks for the **sum**.
∴ 2 cos nα.

The number w = (−1 + √3 i)/2 is a **complex cube root of unity**, usually written ω, and
the identity **1 + ω + ω² = 0** collapses the bracket.
**Step 1 — confirm w is a cube root of unity.**
w² = [(−1 + √3 i)/2]² = (1 − 2√3 i − 3)/4 = (−2 − 2√3 i)/4 = **(−1 − √3 i)/2**
and
1 + w + w² = 1 + (−1 + √3 i)/2 + (−1 − √3 i)/2 = 1 + (−2/2) = 1 − 1 = **0** ✓
Also w³ = 1, so w is ω.
**Step 2 — simplify the bracket** using w² = −1 − w:
3 + w + 3w² = 3 + w + 3(−1 − w)
= 3 + w − 3 − 3w
= **−2w**
**Step 3 — raise to the fourth power.**
(−2w)⁴ = (−2)⁴ w⁴ = 16 w⁴
**Step 4 — reduce w⁴** using w³ = 1:
w⁴ = w³ · w = (1)(w) = **w**

The key fact is the **handshake lemma**: in any graph the number of vertices of **odd**
degree is always **even**.
**Why it is true.** Every edge has two ends, so summing the degrees of all vertices counts
each edge **twice**:
**Σ deg(v) = 2 × (number of edges)**
which is an **even** number. The even-degree vertices contribute an even amount to that
sum, so the odd-degree vertices must contribute an even amount too. A sum of **m** odd
numbers is even only when **m is even** ✓
**Step — apply it.** With m the number of odd-degree vertices, **m is even**, and
therefore

and 0·1254 is indeed close to some of them in size. The trap is to attempt the evaluation

**∫₀^(π/2) sinⁿx dx = ∫₀^(π/2) cosⁿx dx** for every n

**subtangent = y / (dy/dx)**

**dy/dt = a sin t**

**Step 3 — simplify using half-angle identities.**

dy/dx = [2 sin(t/2)cos(t/2)]/[2cos²(t/2)] = **tan(t/2)**
**Step 4 — write the subtangent.** With y = a(1 − cos t) = a × 2sin²(t/2):
subtangent = 2a sin²(t/2) / tan(t/2)
= 2a sin²(t/2) × cos(t/2)/sin(t/2)
= **2a sin(t/2) cos(t/2)**
**Step 5 — fold it back into a single sine.**
= a × 2 sin(t/2)cos(t/2)
= **a sin t** ✓
**Check at t = π/2.**
y = a(1 − 0) = **a**, and dy/dx = tan(π/4) = **1**
subtangent = a/1 = **a**, and the formula gives a sin(π/2) = **a** ✓
**Check at t = π/3.**

subtangent = 0·5a/0·5774 = **0·866a**, and a sin(π/3) = **0·866a** ✓
**What the curve is.** x = a(t + sin t), y = a(1 − cos t) is a **cycloid** — the path
traced by a point on the rim of a rolling circle of radius a. Its gradient tan(t/2) shows
the tangent turning steadily as the circle rolls, and the cusps occur where
t is an odd multiple of π, with dy/dx becoming infinite there.
